June 29: Prepping for Fireworks, Barbeques, Parades and History
Friends,
Happy July 4th, 250th Birthday Week. It’s hard to believe but Saturday is the long-awaited celebration. Hope you are doing something fun somewhere to enjoy the milestone birthday.
Last week was busy with the major DOE $17 billion nuclear loan announcement for Westinghouse/Cameco/Brookfield to develop long-lead time equipment to supply 10 AP1000 reactors. What may have slipped under your radar was 17 EU Member States supporting a statement to postpone the implementation of its methane regulations for three years and the HVACR industry seeking an injunction over the EPA’s refrigerant rule. (see some detail below)
The Senate is out, but the House is expected to be in for the early part of the week but even that remains uncertain. They could potentially vote on NDAA which does have a number of energy provisions, including one focused on DoD delays on renewable project permits. They are also expected to vote on the Securing Community Upgrades for a Resilient (SECURE) Grid Act, which would have states update their energy security plans to include improvements to the physical security and cybersecurity of local distribution systems. They will also vote on legislation to create a Senate-confirmed position at DOE to assess and prevent grid cyberthreats. We also know that House Commerce will hold a manufacturing/technology/innovation hearing tomorrow afternoon with US Chamber Energy Institute head Marty Durbin testifying.
The Supreme Court will likely release a batch of opinions today after which there will only be one such day of announcements remaining this term.
Today at 1:00 p.m., the Joseph Rainey Center for Public Policy holds a virtual town hall on the future of American Energy and permitting featuring Sen. John Curtis (R-UT) policy leaders, and state legislative leaders. Other events include the IEA Annual Global Conference on Energy Efficiency today and tomorrow in Montreal. On Wednesday, a US Energy Association and Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America virtual discussion looks at how rising energy costs are hitting beverage distributors and Cato Institute holds virtual forum on the potential dilemmas about data centers.
Finally, good luck to our friend Heather Reams who is leaving CRES after more than 10 years. She is great leader for the conservative clean energy movement and I suspect she will continue to play an important role on these issues.
Call with questions.
Best,
Frank Maisano

FRANKLY SPOKEN
“I say this not as a threat, but as a statement of duty.”
FERC Commissioner David LaCerte outlining the potential solutions it may impose if RTOs fail to address large-load concerns identified by the agency.
ON THE PODCAST
China’s Impact on Global Oil Market – In this week’s Shift Key podcast, host Robbie Meyer chats with oil analyst Rory Johnston as he walks him through the wonky details of how China helped soften the market blow of the Iran conflict. Although it might seem technical, the implications of that silent intervention are huge for geopolitics, climate policy, and the future of the oil market.
Energy Shots Tackles Jones Act – In this episode of the CSIS’s Energy Shots podcast, hosts Kevin Book and Joe Majkut digs into the Jones Act and where it meets the Hormuz Crisis. The episode looks at the conflict, energy and the implications of protectionism.
FUN OPINIONS
McCormick, Reams Highlight Nuclear Future – In an op-ed in the Washington Examiner, CRES head Heather Reams highlight the work and visit lead by PA Senator Dave McCormick at the Crane Energy Center and why nuclear energy will play an important role in helping America generate the power it needs. It is not just a story about one facility in Pennsylvania. It’s a glimpse of what America’s energy future could look like if we’re willing to build it.
FROG BLOG
Armstrong: Permit Reform Vital to getting American Moving – In an op-ed in the Hill, Sen. Alanm Armstrong says the biggest driver of high energy costs for many Americans isn’t foreign conflict; it is domestic failure to get permitting reform done. The U.S. is an energy superpower, producing more oil and natural gas than any country in the world. Yet millions of Americans pay prices that resemble those in energy-scarce regions because we lack the infrastructure to deliver that supply. The data illustrates this disconnect clearly. In Pennsylvania, one of the most prolific natural gas regions in the world, supply is abundant and inexpensive. However, just 120 miles away in Massachusetts, they pay 252 percent more than the national average. Consumers there might pay $9.70 per unit versus $2.75 nationally.
FUN FACTS
Amazon, Google and Microsoft dominate data centers: New data underscores just how dominant Amazon, Google and Microsoft are when it comes to data centers in North America.
On another front, AGA’s Richard Meyer recreated this chart but included a range of assumptions for the gas turbine capex. The story holds even if turbine costs increase.
IN THE NEWS
DOE Provide $17.5B Loan Guarantees for New Nuclear – The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) issued a conditional loan commitment to finance the purchase of long-lead time items needed to rebuild America’s commercial nuclear supply chain. The $17.5 billion for the American Nuclear Supply Chain Loans will help finance five eligible projects sponsored by utilities and energy companies nationwide to accelerate the deployment of 10 large-scale commercial nuclear reactors across the United States by up to three years.
“Just over one year ago, President Trump directed the Energy Department and its agency partners to unleash the next American nuclear renaissance,” Secretary Wright said. “To accomplish that mission, this conditional loan will play an important role in reviving the supply chain needed for America to once again build large-scale commercial reactors. It will also help accelerate the timeline of building those large-scale reactors by up to three years, lowering construction costs and ensuring the United States is able to deliver on President Trump’s bold and ambitious energy addition agenda.”
Westinghouse’s AP1000® units are the only licensed large-scale advanced commercial reactors operating in the United States today. Long-lead items are complex components of a nuclear power plant that require the longest time for manufacturing and delivery. Westinghouse is owned by Cameco and Brookfield. Here is a release and statement from Cameco CEO Tim Gitzel:
“We are pleased to see the US government make this additional commitment to expanding nuclear power capacity using the proven AP1000 reactor technology,. When combined with the May 23, 2025 Executive Orders and other US government initiatives, we believe the right incentives are being created to advance the rapid deployment of AP1000 reactors in the US. The expansion of nuclear power in the United States is expected to create significant opportunities for Westinghouse and Cameco, accelerating growth in Westinghouse’s energy systems segment during the procurement and subsequent construction phase.”
While this conditional commitment indicates the DOE’s intent to provide a loan to finance these projects, Westinghouse, its owners, and its partners must satisfy certain technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before DOE enters into definitive financing documents and funds the loan.

17 EU Nations Vote to Delay Methane Regs – In a major development, 17 EU Member States supported a statement to postpone the implementation of EUMR for 3 years both by signing the statement and oral interventions at the Council Meeting. The countries include Austria (AT), Belgium (BE), Bulgaria (BG), Czechia (CZ), Germany (DE), Greece (EL), Hungary (HU), Italy (IT), Lithuania (LT), Latvia (LV), Malta (MT), Netherlands (NL), Poland (PL), Romania (RO), Sweden (SE), Slovenia (SI), Slovakia (SK).
German Economy Minister said, “As it stands, the methane regulation would prevent not only gas imports into Germany - LNG - but also petroleum products from being imported from 2027 onwards.”
In the face of opposition to the planned rules from some member states, the European Commission has also drafted plans to waive penalties for companies that breach the rules. EU energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen said on Friday that Brussels was willing to make it easier to implement the rules, but the law - a key pillar of the Commission’s climate agenda - was already flexible enough and the EU would not rewrite it.
CRES Leader Steps Down – WASHINGTON – Today, the Boards of Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions (CRES) and CRES Forum announced that Heather Reams has stepped down as President and CEO. Heather led the organization for a decade marked by a period of strategic growth and national impact.
“Over the past decade, it’s been immensely rewarding to have built a first-of-a-kind conservative energy advocacy organization that is respected inside and outside of the Beltway. Serving as President and CEO at CRES has offered me tremendous opportunities to champion American homegrown energy and become a leading authority on commonsense energy policy. I am also proud of building and leading a senior leadership team and creating and directing enterprise level strategy across government relations, communications, policy, and external affairs,” said Heather Reams. “The energy landscape is changing quickly, and I will continue to work in this ever-evolving, dynamic environment.”
Heather built a foundation of effective advocacy and relationship building across Washington, D.C. During her time at CRES and CRES Forum she created and launched National Clean Energy Week, CRES Academy, CRES Energy Leadership Summit, CRES Clean Energy Champions, and C6WC – a one-of-a-kind platform to engage Republican communicators on Capitol Hill. The Boards will begin an executive search process, and in the interim, day-to-day operations will be led by James Dozier.
HVACR Groups Seek Review on Refrigerant Rule – AHRI The Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) filed a petition Friday for judicial review in the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit arguing that EPA did not follow required procedures in developing the Technology Transitions Reconsideration Final Rule, 91 Fed. Reg. 31,284, issued May 26, 2026. AHRI, which represents manufacturers of air conditioning, heating, commercial refrigeration, and water heating equipment, stressed that its opposition to the rule centered primarily on the EPA’s lack of proper procedure in the rule’s formulation, arguing that it could set a potentially harmful precedent for future federal rulemakings.
“While AHRI and its member companies respect and agree with the Trump Administration’s goal of reducing economic burden and increasing consumer affordability, we take issue with the way this rule was developed. The American Innovation and Manufacturing Act (AIM Act) established specific criteria for rulemakings related to its implementation,” said AHRI President & CEO Stephen Yurek. “Those include proper economic analysis and a compliance lead time of at least one year. Neither of those criteria were followed in this case,” he added.
The Alliance for Responsible Atmospheric Policy noted the considerable efforts of manufacturers in preparing for an efficient transition to lower-GWP refrigerants.
Armstrong Convenes Leaders, Introduces Permitting Legislation – Senator Alan Armstrong convened “Getting America Building Again: Permitting Reform and America’s Competitive Future,” on Capitol Hill, bringing together an executive audience of more than 150 attendees alongside a bipartisan, bicameral coalition of federal and state policymakers. The discussion highlighted the growing consensus that America’s broken permitting system has become one of the greatest obstacles to building critical infrastructure, expanding domestic manufacturing, and strengthening our nation’s economic competitiveness. Those speaking included Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt, Senator John Barrasso (R-WY), Senator Cynthia Lummis (R-WY), Senator Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Senator Peter Welch (D-VT), Senator Jon Husted (R-OH), Senator Steve Daines (R-MT), Congressman Troy Balderson (OH-12), Congressman Mike Collins (GA-10), Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks (IA-01), and Congressman Pete Stauber (MN-08). A panel of experts also discussed permitting including Karen Harbert, President and CEO of the American Gas Association; Ray Long, President and CEO of ACORE; Brandon Farris, EVP of the Steel Manufacturers Association; and Michael Carr, Executive Director of the Solar Energy Manufacturers for America (SEMA) Coalition. See the press release and the video of the full event.
Senator Armstrong, joined by Senators Rick Scott (R-FL), Cynthia Lummis (R-WY), Katie Britt (R-AL), and James Lankford (R-OK), introduced the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act, comprehensive legislation to modernize the federal permitting process while maintaining strong environmental protections. The legislation would establish a faster, more predictable, and more accountable permitting system by reducing unnecessary delays, curbing frivolous litigation, and providing greater certainty for businesses investing in American infrastructure. For more information, here’s a press release, bill text, and one-pager.
ON THE SCHEDULE THIS WEEK
IEA Energy Efficiency Event Set for Montreal – The IEA Annual Global Conference on Energy Efficiency is set for today and tomorrow in Montreal. It is the leading international forum for advancing energy efficiency. Each year, it brings together ministers, CEOs, and senior leaders from government, finance, and business sectors across the globe. Canada and the IEA will co-host the 11th edition with over 600 participants for two days of high-level panels, roundtables and meetings to drive progress forward.
Aspen Ideas Festival Rolls to End Thursday – The Aspen Ideas Festival is finishing up this week in Colorado. There are a number of energy-related events
Curtis Headlines Rainey Center Forum on Permitting – Today at 1:00 p.m., the Joseph Rainey Center for Public Policy holds a virtual town hall on the future of American Energy and permitting featuring Sen. John Curtis (R-UT) policy leaders, and state legislative leaders. The conversation will be a behind-the-scenes look at how federal and state policymakers can work together to strengthen America’s energy future while empowering states to move critical infrastructure forward.
Forum Looks at Affordability – In the second webinar of Advance Energy United’s three-part Energy Affordability series today at 3:00 p.m., industry experts from Dominion Energy and GoodLeap will explore how advanced energy companies are working collaboratively with utilities to manage rising energy costs. Attendees will gain insights into how advanced energy technologies, both grid-scale and distributed, are providing the affordability solutions that customers are searching for. GoodLeap’s Courtney Welch and Dominion’s Nathan Frost speak.
Forum Looks at Eurasia – The Center for the National Interest hosts a seminar tomorrow at 9:00 a.m. looking at a path-breaking article in The National Interest by Eldaniz Gusseinov and Vlad Paddack “Geo-Connectivity and the Death of Eurasia.” In moments of crisis, the connections that bind Eurasia’s economies together can become the very channels through which instability spreads. Geo-connectivity maps the overlapping networks through which geopolitical shocks travel, including pipelines, ports, supply chains, financial flows, and institutional linkages.
Forum Looks at Aligning Capital for Utilities – Energy Central holds a webinar tomorrow at 1:00 p.m. looking at why utilities are aligning Capital, O&M and data initiatives to improve program outcomes.
Chamber’s Durbin Headlines House Energy Look at Manufacturing, Technology – The House Energy and Commerce Committee’s Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee holds a hearing tomorrow at 2:00 p.m. on “American Global Competitiveness at 250: Legislative Proposals to Secure U.S. Technology Leadership. Chamber of Commerce Energy Head Marty Durbin testifies.
Academies to Release Drought Report – The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine holds a virtual event tomorrow at 3:00 p.m. to release its report “The Future of Drought in the United States.” This consensus study committee will consider approaches to understanding and assessing drought in the United States. This review will encompass data sources, metrics, and indicators for characterizing drought in the context of changing drought baselines and trends.
Forum Looks at Current Events, AI – On Wednesday at 8:30 a.m., Punchbowl News holds a discussion on the news of the day, AI infrastructure, small business and the American workforce. Punchbowl News Founder and CEO Anna Palmer will be sitting down with House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie.
USEA Looks at Beverage Industry Impacts of Energy – The US Energy Association; and Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America hold a virtual discussion on Wednesday at 1:00 p.m., on how rising energy costs are hitting beverage distributors. The event looks at how fuel volatility, grid reliability, infrastructure policy and fleet realities are affecting distributors across the country.
House Science Looks at Space Weather Impacts – The House Science Committee holds a hearing on Wednesday at 10:00 a.m. focused on advancing America’s Space Weather capabilities.
Cato Forum Looks at Data Centers – The Cato Institute holds a virtual forum on Wednesday at 1:30 p.m., on the potential dilemmas about data centers. This policy forum will explore the critical role data centers play in technology and innovation. It will also examine how to address key concerns at the heart of critics’ complaints, such as power grid strain and the economic impact of AI, with policy approaches that provide lasting solutions while also securing America’s technological future.
NOAA, Commerce Holds Hearing on Deep Sea Mineral Action – On Wednesday at 3:00 p.m., the Commerce Department and NOAA holds a virtual hearing on American Deep-Sea Minerals, Inc.’s application to conduct seabed mining exploration activities that is fully compliant with the applicable information requirements of the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act and the act’s implementing regulations.
Forum Focused on Hydrogen Vehicles – The Center for European Policy Analysis holds a policy forum on Wednesday at 4:00 p.m. on Hydrogen fuel technology and how it is driving Transatlantic innovation. Featured speakers include BMW’s Josef Hochreiter, Rachel McCleery of SAFE’s Coalition for Reimagined Mobility, FCHEA head Frank Wolak and CEPA’s Ronan Murphy.
JULY 4th – Saturday, 250th US Birthday Celebration
IN THE FUTURE
RFF Looks at Energy Transition in Energy Communities – Resources for the Future holds an event on Tuesday July 7th at 3:00 p.m. as part of a webinar series hosted by RFF’s Resilient Energy Economies initiative focusing on public opinion on energy transition and economic development in energy intensive communities. The event includes insights from two leading researchers’ work across 18 states, the Navajo Nation, and the Jicarilla Apache Nation.
BCSE Talks Data Center Growth – On Wednesday July 15th at 9:00 a.m., the Business Council for Sustainable Energy’s American Energy Abundance Alliance, Fordwell Strategies and Tuli Public Affairs hold an interactive discussion examining the scale and pace of data center growth and the significant energy needs accompanying that expansion. This event will bring together leaders from across the energy sector and the data center industry, to focus on how partnerships can help meet rising demand while advancing reliability, affordability, and sustainability goals.
FERC Technical Conference Set – FERC holds its technical conference focused on actionable reforms to PJM’s stakeholder process and governance will be held on July 23rd. The conference will look to identify and evaluate reforms to improve PJM’s ability to address operational and market needs in a timely and efficient manner.
CEN Sets Energy Summit for Boston – Conservative Energy Network at the third annual National Conservative Energy Summit on August 3rd to 5th in Boston, MA. This event gathers local, state, and federal policymakers, industry leaders, and grassroots advocates from across the country to explore the future of energy policy in America.
